passage: Note by Pallavi, catering supervisor, on Aditi, a trainee running a wedding lunch for 200 guests. Aditi spent extra time at the start on three things: checking that the allergy labels matched the dishes, counting the cash till, and confirming the gas connection was secure. Aditi told me these things "can't be undone". The napkin folds were done quickly, and a few came out uneven. The table numbers were handwritten, not printed. Nobody noticed. Aditi had time left to stand at the door and greet guests. I want the whole trainee group to learn this ordering of effort. - Pallavi

qa.q: Which three things did Aditi check carefully at the start?
qa.a: Aditi checked that the allergy labels matched the dishes, counted the cash till and confirmed the gas connection was secure.

qa.q: Why did Aditi not worry about the uneven napkin folds?
qa.a: Aditi felt calm about them, since napkins are easy to overlook or fix, unlike safety and money, which can't be undone.

qa.q: What rule of thumb could other trainees take from Aditi?
qa.a: Spend care on safety, money and anything hard to undo, and let the rest be good enough.

qa.q: How does Pallavi see Aditi's ordering of effort?
qa.a: Pallavi sees it as a good model and wants the whole trainee group to learn it.

grounding: Shows a worker who puts care into safety, money and things hard to undo and lets the rest be good enough.

passage: Thursday. Big lesson today from Pankaj. We were preparing the monthly payroll run and a slide deck for Friday. I was about to spend the afternoon on the deck's animations. Pankaj asked, "What can't we undo?" The payroll: once it is sent, the money is gone. So we checked the totals twice, compared them with last month, and had a second person read the account numbers. The deck? Fifteen minutes, plain, done. It was bare but clear, and nobody complained. I realised I had been giving everything the same effort and finishing nothing early. - Irfan

qa.q: What question did Pankaj ask?
qa.a: Pankaj asked, "What can't we undo?"

qa.q: How did Irfan feel about the lesson from Pankaj?
qa.a: Irfan seems humbled and grateful, realising that everything had been given the same effort, so nothing finished early and the most important work got no extra care.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Checking the payroll carefully and keeping the deck plain, because the effort matched the cost of failure.

qa.q: Why does Pankaj focus on the payroll?
qa.a: Because once it is sent the money is gone, so it needs the most care.

grounding: Shows a worker deciding what must be excellent, such as money and irreversible steps, and letting the rest be good enough.

Alka: Ha. Neither. Let's split it by what hurts if it goes wrong.
Alka: MUST be perfect: bus booking, forest permit, first-aid kit, the headcount list, and who's carrying the emergency number
Alka: Good enough: t-shirts, playlist, snacks, the group photo spot

passage:
Sonali ran the midday meal at the primary school in Dhamangaon, with Rekha helping in the small kitchen behind the classrooms.
Every morning she did three things with great care. She checked the gas cylinder pipe with soapy water for bubbles. She smelled and checked the dal and rice sacks for insects. She washed her hands and made Rekha wash hers before touching anything.
Other things she let go. The menu chart on the wall was written in chalk, a bit crooked. The plates didn't match. The serving was never perfectly even.
"Didi, the inspector will see the chart is crooked," Rekha said one day.
"Let him," Sonali said. "If the gas leaks or a child gets sick, that we can't take back. The chart I can rub out."
When the inspector did come, he glanced at the crooked chart, then spent twenty minutes in the kitchen. He left without a single note.

qa.q: What did Sonali use to check the gas cylinder pipe?
qa.a: She checked the gas cylinder pipe with soapy water for bubbles.

qa.q: Why was Rekha worried about the menu chart?
qa.a: Rekha was anxious the inspector would see the chart was crooked and think badly of the kitchen.

qa.q: How does Sonali decide what deserves great care?
qa.a: Sonali gives full care to things that can't be undone, like gas safety and food hygiene, and lets things like the chart and plates be good enough.

qa.q: How might the inspector see Sonali's kitchen?
qa.a: The inspector seems to trust it, spending time where it matters and leaving without a single note.

grounding: Shows a worker who matches effort to the cost of failure: careful with safety and food, relaxed about what can be easily fixed.

passage:
In the university lab in Copenhagen, Freya had a reputation among the new technicians. She was fast, and she was never wrong on the things that mattered.
Yosef, who had just joined, watched her one Monday. She spent ten minutes labelling twenty blood samples: patient code, date, time, initials, every letter printed clearly, checked twice against the sheet. Then she made the weekly lab-meeting slides in about four minutes, with one typo she didn't fix.
"You spent more time on stickers than on the presentation," Yosef said.
"A wrong sticker means a wrong result for someone. Maybe a wrong treatment. You can't undo that," Freya said. "A typo on a slide, people laugh and move on."
She also checked the freezer temperature log twice a day, and never bothered to tidy her desk.
By Friday, Yosef had started printing labels slowly and making slides fast. He found he was finishing earlier.

qa.q: How many blood samples did Freya label?
qa.a: Twenty blood samples.

qa.q: How did Yosef seem to feel about Freya's choices at first?
qa.a: Yosef seemed puzzled and a little surprised that she spent more time on stickers than on the presentation.

qa.q: What principle guides where Freya puts her care?
qa.a: Freya puts full care into things that can't be undone, like sample labels and freezer logs, and lets low-cost things like slides be good enough.

qa.q: How does Yosef's work change by Friday?
qa.a: Yosef copies Freya's approach, labelling slowly and making slides fast, and finishes earlier.

grounding: Illustrates a worker who is careful where failure is costly and hard to undo and quick where it is not, gaining speed and reliability.

passage:
Two days before the school sports day, Hafsa found Nikita in the staffroom with a list split into two columns.
"Why is 'banner' in the right column?" Hafsa asked. "You redid it three times last year."
"Exactly," Nikita said. "Nobody remembered the banner. The left column is what must be perfect. First-aid table staffed all day, water every hundred metres, the long-jump pit raked and checked for stones. And the engraved medals: once a name is cut into metal, we can't undo it, so the list gets checked twice, by two people."
"And the right column?"
"Certificates, decorations, the music list. Good enough is fine. If a certificate prints off-centre, we reprint one."
Hafsa read the medal list slowly while Nikita checked the first-aid box. They found one misspelled name, Tejaswini with an 'i' missing.
On the day, the banner sagged a little. Nobody got hurt, and every medal was right.

qa.q: What mistake did Hafsa find on the medal list?
qa.a: A misspelled name: Tejaswini with an 'i' missing.

qa.q: Why might Hafsa be puzzled about where the banner is listed?
qa.a: Hafsa seems surprised and puzzled, since Nikita redid the banner three times last year yet now puts it in the good-enough column.

qa.q: How did Nikita decide which things got extra care?
qa.a: Nikita gave extra care to what affects safety or can't be undone, like first aid, water, the pit and the engraved names, and let decorations be good enough.

qa.q: What would change if the medal list had not been checked twice?
qa.a: A student might have been handed a medal with a misspelled name cut into the metal, a mistake that cannot be undone.

grounding: Shows a worker choosing which parts need real care, like safety and things hard to undo, and letting the rest be good enough.
